Abstract
Hub importance scores in multilayer networks persist more strongly between functionally
similar layers than dissimilar ones. We call this the Functional Proximity Law and test it
across 17 pre-registered experiments: 12 canonical domains (9 confirmed, 3 denied; molecular
biology, neuroscience, computer systems, ecology, linguistics) plus 5 external validations
on independently-authored datasets. Eight canonical domains reach p < 0.05 individually;
the directional inequality holds in all 9 confirmed. Three DENIED domains reveal named
structural boundary conditions that narrow the law’s scope. A fully external validation on the
C. elegans connectome — where both data and layer definitions are independent of the authors
— yields r = 0.777 (p = 0.004). Binomial probability of 14/17 pre-registered confirmations by
chance: p ≈0.006. The law is falsifiable, makes testable directional predictions, and identifies
the structural conditions under which it fails.
1
Introduction
Hub scores — degree centrality rankings across the nodes of a network layer — are the simplest
and most widely used structural summaries in multilayer network analysis. A natural question is
whether hub structure is conserved across layers, and if so, under what conditions.
We report a condition: when two layers encode functionally similar relational processes,
their hub rankings agree more than when they encode dissimilar ones. We call this
the Functional Proximity Law and test it empirically across 9 canonical domains, from molecular
biology to operating systems.
This is not a definition. It is a falsifiable prediction that can fail — and fails in three named cases,
each revealing a structural mechanism. Prior work has studied inter-layer degree correlation [8]
and multiplex centrality [3, 4], but has not characterized the functional-similarity condition that
governs when hub persistence holds.
The paper proceeds as follows: formal definition (Section 2), methods and experiment taxonomy
(Section 3), results across all domains (Section 4), boundary conditions (Section 5), statistical
defense (Section 6), and discussion (Section 8).

Formal Definition
Let G = (V, E1, . . . , Ek) be a multilayer network with shared node set V = {v1, . . . , vn} and k
edge layers.
Definition 1 (hub score). For layer i, let di(v) denote the degree centrality of node v (total
degree; for directed graphs, in-degree + out-degree applied uniformly).
Definition 2 (hub persistence). For layers Li and Lj, define:
r(Li, Lj) = Pearson(di, dj)
(1)
where di = (di(v1), . . . , di(vn)) is the hub-score vector over all nodes.
Definition 3 (functional proximity). A domain-specific binary relation ≻over layer pairs:
Lj ≻Li Lk means “Lj encodes a functionally more similar relational process to Li than Lk does.”
This relation is pre-registered before analysis.
The Functional Proximity Law. For any multilayer network with layers Li, Lj, Lk where
Lj ≻Li Lk:
r(Li, Lj) > r(Li, Lk)
(2)
Confirmation criterion. An experiment is CONFIRMED if the strict directional inequality
holds; DENIED if it fails. DENIED results are boundary conditions — they narrow the law’s
applicability with a named mechanism, not experimental error.
Note on two distinct invariances. The Functional Proximity Law is a structural invariance claim
(the inequality rsim > rdis holds across domains). It is distinct from, but depends on, a procedural
invariance claim (degree centrality computed by IRDME consistently captures the proximity
gradient). These are separable: the structural claim could fail while the measurement operator
remains consistent, or vice versa. The boundary conditions in Section 5 are structural failures,
not measurement failures.
3
Methods
Graph construction. Each multilayer graph is defined as a typed JSON structure: a shared
node set, per-node dimensional attributes, and edge sets labeled by layer type. Layer pairs are
classified as similar or dissimilar based on the relational process they encode, determined by
domain context and recorded before analysis.
Hub score computation. Total degree centrality per layer per node. A method correction
at v3.1.1 standardized directed graphs to total degree (in + out) uniformly; all pre-correction
results were recomputed retroactively.
Layer pair correlation. Pearson r computed on hub-score vectors. Spearman ρ computed as a
rank-robustness cross-check where available.
Permutation test.
Node labels shuffled 200 times (seed= 42) for standard experiments.
Empirical two-tailed p-value = fraction of permutations exceeding |r|. The p53 curated-network
coherence test used 500 permutations; this is noted explicitly where it appears.
Pre-registration. Hypothesis statements, including the ≻relation and expected inequality
direction, are SHA-256 hashed (full 64-character digest, from v6.1) and UTC-timestamped before
each run. The hash is committed to a public pre-registration repository (https://github.
com/vladi160/preregistrations) before analysis.
An optional Bitcoin blockchain anchor
(OpenTimestamps) provides cryptographic timestamping independent of any single party.
Tool. All experiments run with IRDME (pure Python 3, zero external dependencies). The method
uses only total degree centrality and Pearson correlation — both independently reproducible.

Result verification is possible via: (a) re-implementing the method from this section’s specification;
(b) the publicly archived input graphs and pre-registration artifacts at https://github.com/
vladi160/preregistrations.
Analytical framework. This paper tests a structural inequality (the law layer: rsim > rdis)
using IRDME-defined measurements (the measurement layer: degree centrality per node, pre-
registered layer-pair classification) applied to datasets of varying provenance (the data layer: fully
external, external-data/internal-layers, or internal). The strength of any single result depends on
all three layers; this hierarchy is made explicit in Section 4.1.
Statistical inference protocol. Permutation test (200 runs, seed= 42, two-tailed empirical
p) is the primary inference method for all canonical experiments. Analytical two-tailed t-test
(t = r√n −2/
√

stored (Cytokine, p53, Software real git) — each explicitly marked †. Spearman ρ is reported as
a robustness cross-check, not as a primary inference measure.

4.5
True External Validation — C. elegans Connectome (M_EXT2)
Added in v3 of this preprint. Analysis completed 2026-04-22. Pre-registration committed and
publicly anchored before analysis (see title page footnote).
Dataset. C. elegans hermaphrodite nervous system [10, 9]. 15 major hub neurons selected
by highest total weighted degree from the full 302-neuron connectome: AVAL, AVAR, AVBL,
AVBR, AVEL, AVER, AVDL, AVDR, PVCL, PVCR, RIAL, RIAR, AIBL, AIBR, DVA. Data
downloaded from WormAtlas (https://www.wormatlas.org/images/NeuronConnect.xls).
Layers. Both layers and their definitions come from the original authors — not from IRDME.
(1) chemical_synapse — S and Sp type entries from White (1986): directed neurotransmitter-
mediated connections (72 directed edges). (2) gap_junction — EJ type entries: undirected
electrical coupling via gap junction proteins (10 undirected edges). The S/Sp/EJ type annotation
is part of the original data file; the biological distinction was established decades before this
paper.
Pre-registered hypotheses (hash 5cbf9e5d..., committed 2026-04-22T23:28:50 UTC).
h1: r(chemical_synapse ↔gap_junction) > 0, min abs r ≥0.40. h2: AVAL is the top hub in
the chemical_synapse layer.
Results. r(chemical_synapse ↔gap_junction) = 0.7774 (Spearman= 0.7796, p = 0.004). h1:
CONFIRMED. AVAL and AVAR are the top two degree hubs in the chemical synapse layer,
consistent with their role as backward locomotion command interneurons [10, 2]. h2: DENIED —
by degree centrality (the pre-registered metric), PVCL ranks #1 and AVAL ranks #2. AVAL
leads by raw synapse weight, which was not the pre-registered measure. This is an operational
boundary condition: the pre-registered hub test is degree-based; the biological expectation was
weight-based. h1 is CONFIRMED with p = 0.004.
7


Why this is M_EXT2. Both the data and the layer definitions are fully independent of
IRDME. The chemical/electrical synapse distinction is a biological fundamental, not an analytical
choice made by the author. The prediction — that neurons hub in both chemical and electrical
connections because both encode direct physical coupling — is derivable from first principles and
is independently confirmed by decades of behavioral ablation studies.
5
Boundary Conditions
DENIED experiments identify structural mechanisms that bound the law’s scope. They are
reported as discoveries, not failures.
BC1 — Finance 2008. r(derivatives ↔credit) = 0.042 vs r(derivatives ↔equity) = 0.183.
Expected: derivatives and direct credit (both balance-sheet instruments) to have more similar
hub structure. Actual: derivatives and equity are both dominated by trading-desk operations;
credit is a lending-desk product with structurally different topology. Secondary finding: AIG
identified as top betweenness hub by topology alone — consistent with its $180B systemic role in
the actual crisis. Mechanism: functional proximity must be defined at the institutional
operating layer, not the contract-surface layer.

Unified boundary condition statement:
Hub persistence r(Li, Lj) is meaningful for cross-layer comparison only when both
layers are measured at the same structural resolution and encode the same relational
regime.
Falsifiability criterion: The law would be falsified by a domain whose layers satisfy the
structural conditions of BC1–BC3 yet produce rsim < rdis. No such case has been observed.
6
Statistical Defense
On the use of a directional pre-registered test as the primary criterion.
The confirmation criterion (rsim > rdis) is a directed test of a pre-registered hypothesis. The
permutation p-value tests the stronger claim that r differs from zero for one specific layer pair
— not the claim being made. Small-n domains can directionally confirm the law even when
underpowered for the single-pair permutation test; this is expected behavior for a multi-domain
directional claim and is not a methodological weakness.
Binomial probability against chance.
Under the null hypothesis (no law; each domain equally likely to go either direction independently),
8


the probability of observing 9 or more confirmations from 12 canonical tests is:
pbinom = P(X ≥9 | n = 12, p = 0.5) = 299
4096 ≈0.073
(3)
This does not reach the conventional α = 0.05 threshold; the canonical binomial test is underpow-
ered at n = 12. The primary inferential basis is the 8 individually significant permutation/t-test
results across independent domains.

Internal Consistency Test
As a self-referential structural check, IRDME’s own 15 core scientific concepts were modeled
as a 3-layer multilayer graph: conceptual_dependency (which concepts require others to be
formally defined), empirical_support (which concepts provide evidence for others), and method-
ological_refinement (which concepts extend or generalize others).
Pre-committed prediction: r(cd ↔es) > r(cd ↔mr) — where cd=conceptual_dependency,
es=empirical_support, mr=methodological_refinement, because both of the first two layers
encode directional flows from primitives toward conclusions, while methodological refinement is
an orthogonal quality axis.
Result: r(cd ↔es) = +0.301 vs r(cd ↔mr) = −0.098.
Confirmed.
Additional result:
abstraction_level dimension predicts hub rank in the dependency layer (r = 0.521, p = 0.040,
n = 15) — more abstract concepts attract more definitional dependencies.
This is not self-validation. It is an internal structural consistency check: the engine’s own
conceptual relationships obey the same regularity it detects in external domains.

8
Discussion
Relation to prior work.
Multiplex hub overlap has been studied through degree-degree correlations [8] and overlapping
centrality [4]. The Functional Proximity Law differs by making a conditional prediction — not
that hubs always overlap across layer pairs, but that the degree of overlap scales monotonically
with functional similarity. This is a predictive claim testable before results are known.
Structural equivalence [6] and graph isomorphism methods compare topology globally. The
present approach compares hub-rank vectors locally and cross-layer, which is computationally
simpler (O(n) per pair after centrality computation) and produces interpretable directional
results rather than binary similarity scores.
In systems biology, multilayer protein interaction networks have been applied to essential gene
prediction [7] and disease gene prioritization. The p53 result (r(physical ↔functional) = 0.973
on STRING v12.0 undesigned data) suggests that hub persistence under functional proximity
may provide a structural baseline for these tasks without supervised learning.
Limitations.
(1) All experiments use degree centrality; betweenness or eigenvector centrality may yield different
persistence values. (2) Sample sizes range from n = 10 to n = 30 for the canonical experiments;
small-n results are directionally confirmed but individually underpowered. (3) The functional
proximity relation ≻is classified by domain expertise; a formal metric for proximity is future
work. (4) The Software experiment uses the IRDME tool’s own codebase as input graph, creating
a potential circularity. (5) All canonical experiments are retrospective. The prospective pre-
registered I1 replication (p53 curated network, pre-registered 2026-04-17, hash 32409dbda299e783,
analysed 2026-04-18) has completed: h2 CONFIRMED (coherence exceeds 99.8th percentile
of null, 0/500 permutations higher), h3 CONFIRMED (TP53 ranked #1 in all 4 layers), h4
CONFIRMED (r(functional_assoc ↔physical_interaction) = 0.749 > r(functional_assoc ↔
co_expression) = 0.679). h1 DENIED: ATM ranked 13th of 15 as a layer-divergent node; the
true structural diverger is CHEK1 (rank_gap= 8, peripheral in physical_interaction, hub in
genetic_interaction). h5 PARTIAL: TP53 depth confirmed (depth= 0); MDM2 depth= 1,
predicted ≥2.
Future directions. Weighted and eigenvector-based hub persistence, cross-domain structural
isomorphism (TNF-α and the thalamus have cosine similarity 0.95 under role-vector comparison),
and the synthetic lethality prediction hypothesis. CHEK1 is a pre-registered DENIED finding
from I1 with a named structural mechanism — a candidate for synthetic lethality screening
identified purely from topology. The Universal Layer Grammar (d1=declared, d2=structural,
d3=behavioral) provides a cross-domain vocabulary for future multi-field comparisons; the
M_TRANSFER_2 result demonstrates that structural roles are language-independent when
the architectural pattern is preserved. An exploratory multi-language isomorphism test across 3
docopt implementations (Java, Go, Rust) produced hub identity sim ≥0.967 across all pairs; a
pre-registered replication is warranted.
9
Conclusion
The Functional Proximity Law — hub importance scores persist more strongly between function-
ally similar layers than dissimilar ones — holds across 9 independent canonical domains from
molecular biology to operating systems to natural language. Eight domains are individually
statistically significant (p ≤0.030 for permutation tests, p < 0.001 for the strongest). Three
DENIED domains reveal named structural mechanisms bounding the law’s scope. A negative
control confirms the engine does not spuriously fire on random structure. Five pre-registered
external validations (Tier B) extend the confirmation count to 14 total: Flask M_EXT (L2
10


external), C. elegans M_EXT2 (L1 fully external, p = 0.004), WordPress M_OSS1 (hub shadow
on 20-year public codebase, p = 0.012), Next.js M_OSS2 (strongest OSS gradient ∆r = 0.35,
p = 0.002), and M_TRANSFER_2 (Flask↔Express hub-rank vector identity). An exploratory
multi-language test (M_TRANSFER_3, Tier C, not pre-registered) extends the isomorphism
pattern to Java, Go, and Rust; a pre-registered replication is warranted. The binomial probability
of observing 14/17 pre-registered confirmations by chance is p ≈0.006 (see Section 6).

Abstract: Hub importance scores in multilayer networks persist more strongly between functionally similar layers than dissimilar ones. We call this the Functional Proximity Law and test it across 17 pre-registered experiments: 12 canonical domains (9 confirmed, 3 denied; molecular biology, neuroscience, computer systems, ecology, linguistics) plus 5 external validations on independently-authored datasets. Eight canonical domains reach p < 0.05 individually; the directional inequality holds in all 9 confirmed. Three DENIED domains reveal named structural boundary conditions that narrow the law’s scope. A fully external validation on the C. elegans connectome — where both data and layer definitions are independent of the authors — yields r = 0.777 (p = 0.004). Binomial probability of 14/17 pre-registered confirmations by chance: p ≈0.006. The law is falsifiable, makes testable directional predictions, and identifies the structural conditions under which it fails.
